Well, a lot of it has to do with my philosophy on technology in general, that is, that new technologies need to be judged based on their merit compared with the incumbent technology it purports to replace. In this case, Debian is the incumbent, as it has the longest pedigree. So the question becomes, what are the criteria on which you should judge replacement technologies on? The answer to this question is largely dependent on which technology you're talking about, whether its Gentoo, Arch, Fedora, SuSE, etc... By and large, it is my impression that most "new" distributions spring in to existence for one of three reasons: package management, default configuration, or supported hardware.

Taking these three areas (PM, DC, and SH) as the criteria on which to judge "new" distributions, the next question one has to ask is who has the obligation to provide the affirmative defense? Without being condescending, an affirmative defense places the "burden of proof" on whichever party carries the burden to prove its case. In cases such as this, I put the burden of proof on the "new" technology.

In regards to PM (package management), I am convinced you will not find a package management that is not without its faults. That said, I am equally convinced that Debian's package manager is one of, if not the most, robust and well done package managers on the market. Moreover, the only package manager with an even approximately comparable number of packages is the Red Hat Package Manager (RPM), and RPM's are really split across two family trees: Red Hat and SuSE. Mixing RPM family trees is disastrous.

In regards to DC (default configuration), there are two basic sub-criteria: whether the distribution places an emphasis on wide-spread usability or whether it takes the "only what you need" approach, and what technologies are employed "under the hood". Debian strikes what I consider to be a reasonable balance in regards to the first sub-criteria. In regards to the second sub-criteria, you can call me a stuffy old curmudgeon, but I LOATHE upstart and systemd, just one example of the technology employed "under the hood". Other "under the hood" examples would be whether the system implements SELinux, X11, XFree86, XOrg, how it lays out the filesystem (LFS or some renegade layout?), what boot loader it uses, etc., etc., etc.

Supported Hardware (SH) could reasonably be argued as a non-starter as all hardware support is dependent on the Kernel, which is a fair point, but... there are cases, such as with Intel's wireless chip set, for which support is not included in Debian because of its social contract that requires included packages be "free" (as in GPL, or similar.) So, the default inclusion of things like nVidia or ATI drivers, or similar may not be included. So, with regards to Debian this is a strike against it on account of the fact that a lot of systems simply won't work without these "non-free" drivers, so...

At any rate, these are the criteria against which I judge a distribution, and based on these, I am staunchly a proponent of Debian. That said, I continue to evaluate all new-comers. I've played with virtually every "major" distribution (e.g. the top 20 on distrowatch.com.) That said, I have three laptops and a couple of servers: my battlestation runs Kali, my main lappy runs Debian 8.1, one of my servers runs CentOS 6 and the other runs Debian 8.0. For the record, Kali is Debian-based, and my CentOS box exists almost exclusively for the purpose of running an SS5 proxy and a shell sever for a couple of friends.

SO, that's a long-winded, round-about answer, but hopefully it serves you.
